quote: Donald Brown once compiled a list of over two hundred “human universals,” found in all (or a vast supermajority of) studied human cultures, from San Francisco to the !Kung of the Kalahari Desert.
content: Brown’s list (Human Universals, 1991, a book with no DOI) is a survey of the ethnographic record, and Brown was explicit that it mixes absolute universals with near-universals and “universals of classification” such as “has some form of X,” which are satisfied trivially; the essay’s next sentence, “no one who knows anything about evolutionary psychology could be expected to deny it,” converts the list into a claim about DNA that the list does not make. A practice found in every culture can be a convergent cultural solution to a shared problem (fire, cooking, containers are universal and not innate), and Norenzayan & Heine (2005) lay out the levels at which a universal can hold, from “available in every mind” to “used in the same way everywhere,” and show that ethnographic presence establishes only the weakest. Some of Brown’s items have since been tested properly and held: music, in the cross-cultural corpus study of Mehr et al. (2019). Others, notably the universality of basic emotion expressions, which is the item the essay’s “strongest emotions... blood and bone” most depends on, did not hold when tested outside the WEIRD sample (Gendron et al. (2014), the Himba study; Book III’s annotations on Ekman). The list is a reasonable place to start and an unreasonable place to stop.

quote: It might take a bit of tweaking, but you probably could tell “Hamlet” sitting around a campfire on the ancestral savanna.
content: The experiment was run. Laura Bohannan told Hamlet to Tiv elders in Nigeria in the 1950s and reported the result in “Shakespeare in the Bush” (Natural History, 1966): the elders rejected the premises one by one. A dead man cannot walk, so the ghost was an omen sent by a witch; Gertrude’s remarriage to her husband’s brother was proper and prompt, not shameful; Hamlet’s duty was not to avenge his father but to leave that to the elders; his madness must have been witchcraft; and Ophelia was drowned by a witch, probably Laertes, who wanted to sell her body. The plot survived and the tragedy did not, because the tragedy lives in the premises. Bohannan’s is a single anecdote, but it is the single anecdote that bears on the sentence, and it came out the other way. The essay concedes the point six paragraphs later (“the Great Stories are not timeless, because the human species is not timeless”) and keeps the savanna Hamlet anyway; the essay wants universality when arguing against the Romantic and historicity when arguing for transhumanism, and it does not notice that the two paragraphs disagree.

quote: No one who knows anything about evolutionary psychology could be expected to deny it: The strongest emotions we have are deeply engraved, blood and bone, brain and DNA.
content: A research program in affective science denies exactly this, and it is not a fringe one. The psychological-constructionist account (Barrett, How Emotions Are Made, 2017; Barrett (2017) in Perspectives on Psychological Science) holds that discrete emotions such as anger and grief are not natural kinds engraved in the brain but concepts assembled from core affect, bodily prediction and culturally supplied categories, and that the cross-cultural evidence for “basic emotions” rests on forced-choice methods that manufacture the agreement they report. The Ekman universals that gave the “blood and bone” picture its empirical basis were the subject of Book III’s annotations, where the free-labelling replications in the Himba and Trobriand samples did not find them. The truth may be between the two camps; but “no one could be expected to deny it” describes a field with a live dispute as a field with a consensus, and the essay’s poetic thesis (Hamlet is intelligible because grief and revenge are universal) needs the strong claim, which is the one under challenge.
